---
title: "Quiz: edges, Gaussian derivatives and Canny"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Convention: $x$ to the right, $y$ down; $L_y$ is the change going down; angles are counter-clockwise on the screen.

---

**Q1.** Why do we smooth an image before taking derivatives? What is lost by smoothing?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does a difference of neighbours do to a pixel that differs from its neighbours?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A derivative is a difference of neighbouring pixels, and noise is exactly pixels that differ from their neighbours: the derivative amplifies it. Smoothing first averages the noise away. The price: edges get wider, corners round off, and edges closer than about 2σ merge into one.
:::

---

**Q2.** A Gaussian kernel with σ = 3 is cut at 4σ. How many taps does it have? How many multiplications per pixel does a 2D blur need, done directly and done separably?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Taps from −4σ to +4σ. Separable: one pass along rows, one along columns.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$2 \cdot 12 + 1 = 25$ taps. Directly $25^2 = 625$ multiplications per pixel; separably $2 \cdot 25 = 50$.
:::

---

**Q3.** "Smooth, then differentiate" needs two filters. Why can it be done with one kernel, and what does that kernel look like?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Applying two kernels one after the other is the same as applying their convolution.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Convolutions combine: applying the Gaussian and then the difference kernel equals applying their convolution once. The result is the derivative of a Gaussian: a positive lobe on one side and a negative lobe on the other, "right minus left, with Gaussian weights". In 2D, $G_x$ is this 1D kernel along $x$ times a plain Gaussian along $y$, like a large, smooth Sobel kernel.
:::

---

**Q4.** At a pixel $L_x = -6$ and $L_y = 8$. What are the edge strength and the gradient direction? Which side of the edge is brighter?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$y$ points down, so $L_y > 0$ means brighter further down.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Strength $\sqrt{36 + 64} = 10$. The gradient points left and down; counter-clockwise on the screen, $\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(-8, -6) = -126.9°$ (or 233.1°). The brighter side is to the lower left. The edge itself runs perpendicular to this, from lower right to upper left.
:::

---

**Q5.** After non-maximum suppression, why is an edge one pixel wide? Which two pixels is a pixel compared with?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Across the edge the magnitude is a ridge.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Across an edge, the gradient magnitude rises to a crest and falls again. NMS keeps a pixel only if its magnitude is at least that of its two neighbours **along the gradient direction** (rounded to 0°, 45°, 90° or 135°), i.e. across the edge. Only the crest pixel survives on each cross-section. Pixels along the edge are not compared with each other, so the edge stays connected.
:::

---

**Q6.** With $t_\text{low} = 4$ and $t_\text{high} = 10$: a pixel of magnitude 6 (after NMS) is kept in one place and removed in another. How can that be?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Hysteresis looks at the neighbours too.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
6 is a weak value (between the thresholds). A weak pixel is kept only if it is connected, through pixels of at least 4, to a seed of at least 10. On a faint stretch of a real edge it hangs on to the strong parts and is kept; as an isolated noise pixel it has no seed and is removed.
:::

---

**Q7.** Canny finds a ragged mess of short edges in a noisy image. Which parameter would you change first, and in which direction?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Noise edges come from small structures.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Increase σ: more smoothing removes the noise before the gradient is taken. (Raising $t_\text{low}$ also removes noise chains, but leaves the edges themselves noisy.) Watch for the price: corners rounding off and close edges merging.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that the derivative of the Gaussian $g_\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}$ is $-\frac{x}{\sigma^2}g_\sigma(x)$. Where are its extremes?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Chain rule; then set the derivative of $x e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}$ to zero.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\frac{d}{dx}e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2} = -\frac{x}{\sigma^2}e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}$, so $g'_\sigma = -\frac{x}{\sigma^2}g_\sigma$. Extremes where $\frac{d}{dx}(x e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}) = (1 - x^2/\sigma^2)e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2} = 0$: at $x = \pm\sigma$. The two lobes of the kernel sit one σ either side of the centre.
:::
